subject: Climate & Environment
title: Apex Predators and Ecosystem Health
description: A 60-second lesson on Apex Predators and Ecosystem Health.

hook.text: Sharks have patrolled the oceans for 450 million years. Now we kill 100 million per year.

buildup.text: Apex predators keep prey populations in check, preventing any one species from dominating.

discovery.text: Without sharks, mid-level predators explode, devouring shellfish and smaller fish stocks.

twist.text: Removing large predators from land has similar effects — deer overgraze, forests thin.

climax.text: Healthy ecosystems need their top predators. Fear alone changes prey behavior for the better.

punchline.text: The animals we fear most are the ones ecosystems need most.

quiz.question: How many sharks are killed by humans each year?

details.summary: Apex predators like wolves, sharks, and lions regulate prey populations and maintain ecosystem balance through top-down control. Their removal causes prey explosions that overgraze vegetation, erode soils, and collapse food webs.
details.whyItMatters: Predator persecution has caused ecological damage worldwide. Recognizing their regulatory role reshapes conservation from predator control to predator protection.
takeaways: Their removal often triggers vegetation collapse and soil erosion
Restoring predators can reverse decades of ecological degradation

faq.question: Why are sharks important for ocean ecosystems?
faq.answer: Sharks control populations of mid-level predators and herbivorous fish, preventing any single species from dominating. Their decline has been linked to seagrass loss, coral reef degradation, and collapsing fish stocks in multiple ocean regions.

faq.question: What happened when wolves were removed from Yellowstone?
faq.answer: Elk populations surged and overgrazed willows and aspens along rivers. Riverbanks eroded, songbird habitat vanished, and beaver populations crashed. Reintroducing wolves in 1995 reversed many of these cascading effects.
